Date: August 4, 2020
Abstract.

We introduce a novel approach to Bertini irreducibility theorems over an arbitrary field, based on random hyperplane slicing over a finite field. Extending a result of Benoist, we prove that for a morphism ϕ:X→ℙn\phi\colon X\to\mathbb{P}^{n} such that XX is geometrically irreducible and the nonempty fibers of ϕ\phi all have the same dimension, the locus of hyperplanes HH such that ϕ−1​H\phi^{-1}H is not geometrically irreducible has dimension at most codim⁡ϕ⁡(X)+1\codim\phi(X)+1. We give an application to monodromy groups above hyperplane sections.

Key words and phrases: 
Bertini irreducibility theorem, Lang–Weil bound, finite field, random hyperplane slicing
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14D05; Secondary 14A10, 14G15.

1. Introduction

Most Bertini theorems state that a moduli space of hyperplanes contains a dense open subset whose points correspond to hyperplanes with some good property, so if the moduli space has dimension nn, the locus of bad hyperplanes has dimension at most n−1n-1. In contrast, we exhibit Bertini theorems in which the bad locus is often much smaller.

1.1. Bertini irreducibility theorems

We work over an arbitrary ground field kk. By variety, we mean a separated scheme of finite type over kk; subvarieties need only be locally closed. Given ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}, let ℙˇn\check{\mathbb{P}}^{n} be the dual projective space, so H∈ℙˇnH\in\check{\mathbb{P}}^{n} means that HH is a hyperplane in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} (over the residue field of the corresponding point). The following is part of a theorem of Olivier Benoist:

Theorem 1.1 (cf. [1]*Théorème 1.4).

Let XX be a geometrically irreducible subvariety of ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} for some n≥0n\geq 0. Let ℳbad⊆ℙˇn\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}}\subseteq\check{\mathbb{P}}^{n} be the constructible locus parametrizing hyperplanes HH such that H∩XH\cap X is not geometrically irreducible. Then dimℳbad≤codim⁡X+1\dim\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}}\leq\codim X+1.

Example 1.2.

For a hypersurface X⊂ℙnX\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}, Theorem 1.1 says dimℳbad≤2\dim\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}}\leq 2.

Remark 1.3.

The bound codim⁡X+1\codim X+1 is best possible: see [1]*Section 3.1.

Remark 1.4.

Benoist assumes that XX is closed and geometrically integral, but these additional hypotheses can easily be removed. In fact, he bounds a larger set ℳbad\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}} that includes also the HH such that H∩XH\cap X is not generically reduced. Additionally, he proves a best possible analogue in which hyperplanes are replaced by hypersurfaces of a fixed degree ee. Benoist’s proof uses a degeneration to a union of hyperplanes.

Our key new observation is that the statistics of random hyperplane slices over a finite field give another way to bound the bad locus in Bertini irreducibility theorems. We were inspired by [9], which used random slicing to give a proof of the Lang–Weil theorem, and by [8], which used random slicing to refine the Lang–Weil bounds for hypersurfaces. Using this approach, we give a new proof of Theorem 1.1, and generalize it to a setting analogous to that in [6]*Théorème 6.3(4):

Theorem 1.5.

Let XX be a geometrically irreducible variety. Let ϕ:X→ℙn\phi\colon X\to\mathbb{P}^{n} be a morphism. Let ℳbad\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}} be the constructible locus parametrizing hyperplanes H⊂ℙnH\subset\mathbb{P}^{n} such that ϕ−1​H\phi^{-1}H is not geometrically irreducible. If the nonempty fibers of ϕ\phi all have the same dimension, then dimℳbad≤codim⁡ϕ⁡(X)+1\dim\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}}\leq\codim\phi(X)+1.

Example 1.6.

In the setting of Theorem 1.5, if ϕ\phi is dominant, then the conclusion states that dimℳbad≤1\dim\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}}\leq 1.

Theorem 1.5 can fail if the nonempty fibers of ϕ\phi have differing dimensions:

Example 1.7.

If X→ℙnX\to\mathbb{P}^{n} is the blow-up of a linear subspace L⊂ℙnL\subset\mathbb{P}^{n} with codim⁡L≥2\codim L\geq 2, then ℳbad\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}} parametrizes the hyperplanes containing LL, so dimℳbad=codim⁡L−1\dim\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}}=\codim L-1, but codim⁡ϕ⁡(X)+1=1\codim\phi(X)+1=1 (so the conclusion of Theorem 1.5 fails if codim⁡L≥3\codim L\geq 3).

Nevertheless, Theorem 1.5 admits the following generalization. Fix an algebraic closure k¯⊃k{\overline{k}}\supset k.

Theorem 1.8.

Let XX be a geometrically irreducible variety. Let ϕ:X→ℙn\phi\colon X\to\mathbb{P}^{n} be a morphism. Let WW be the closed subset of x∈Xx\in X at which the relative dimension dimxϕ\dim_{x}\phi is greater than at the generic point. Let W1,…,WrW_{1},\ldots,W_{r} be the irreducible components of Wk¯W_{{\overline{k}}} of dimension dimX−1\dim X-1. Let ℳbad\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}} be the locus of hyperplanes HH such that ϕ−1​H\phi^{-1}H is not geometrically irreducible. Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be the locus of hyperplanes over k¯{\overline{k}} that contain ϕ⁡(Wi)\phi(W_{i}) for some ii; since {W1,…,Wr}\{W_{1},\ldots,W_{r}\} is Galois-stable, 𝒩\mathcal{N} is definable over kk. Then ℳbad\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}} differs from 𝒩\mathcal{N} in a constructible set of dimension at most codim⁡ϕ⁡(X)+1\codim\phi(X)+1.

1.2. Monodromy

A generically étale morphism ϕ:X→Y\phi\colon X\to Y between integral varieties has a monodromy group Mon⁡(ϕ)\Mon(\phi), defined as the Galois group of the Galois closure of the function field extension k⁡(X)/k⁡(Y)k(X)/k(Y); see Section 8 for a more general definition requiring only YY to be integral. Now suppose Y⊂ℙnY\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}. For a hyperplane H⊂ℙnH\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}, let ϕH\phi_{H} be the restriction ϕ−1​(H∩Y)→H∩Y\phi^{-1}(H\cap Y)\to H\cap Y. The following theorem states that for all H∈ℙˇnH\in\check{\mathbb{P}}^{n} outside a low-dimensional locus, Mon⁡(ϕH)≃Mon⁡(ϕ)\Mon(\phi_{H})\simeq\Mon(\phi).

Theorem 1.9.

Let ϕ:X→Y\phi\colon X\to Y be a generically étale morphism with YY an integral subvariety of ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} over an algebraically closed field. Let ℳgood⊂ℙˇn\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{good}}\subset\check{\mathbb{P}}^{n} be the locus parametrizing hyperplanes HH such that

  1. (i)

    H∩YH\cap Y is irreducible;

  2. (ii)

    the generic point of H∩YH\cap Y has a neighborhood UU in YY such that UU is normal and ϕ−1​U→U\phi^{-1}U\to U is finite étale; and

  3. (iii)

    the inclusion Mon⁡(ϕH)↪Mon⁡(ϕ)\Mon(\phi_{H})\hookrightarrow\Mon(\phi) is an isomorphism.

Then the locus ℳbad:⁣=ℙˇn−ℳgood\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{bad}}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\check{\mathbb{P}}^{n}-\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{good}} is a constructible set of dimension at most codim⁡Y+1\codim Y+1.

Remark 1.10.

Conditions (i) and (ii) are needed to define the inclusion in (iii): see Section 8.

Example 1.11.

Let kk be an algebraically closed field of characteristic not 22, let X=Spec⁡k⁡[x1,…,xn,y]/(y2−x1)X=\Spec k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y]/(y^{2}-x_{1}), and let ϕ:X→𝔸kn⊂ℙn\phi\colon X\to\mathbb{A}^{n}_{k}\subset\mathbb{P}^{n} be the projection to 𝔸kn=Spec⁡k⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbb{A}^{n}_{k}=\Spec k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]. Then ℳbad\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{bad}} is the 11-dimensional locus consisting of the hyperplanes x1=ax_{1}=a for a∈ka\in k.

1.3. Structure of the article

After a brief notation section, Theorem 1.5 is proved in Sections 3 to 6; see especially Lemma 6.1. We apply it to prove Theorems 1.8 and 1.9 in Sections 7 and 8, respectively. The heart of our paper is the random slicing in Section 4 and its application towards irreducibility in Section 6.

2. Notation

The empty scheme is not irreducible. For a noetherian scheme XX, let Irr⁡X\Irr X be the set of irreducible components of XX. If XX is an irreducible variety, let k⁡(X)k(X) be the function field of the associated reduced subscheme XredX_{{\operatorname{red}}}. The dimension of a constructible subset CC of a variety VV (viewed as a topological subspace) equals the maximal dimension of a subvariety of VV contained in CC; then codimC:⁣=dimV−dimC\codim C\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\dim V-\dim C.

Let SS be a scheme, and let XX be an SS-scheme. Given a morphism of schemes T→ST\to S, let XTX_{T} denote X×STX\times_{S}T; in this context, if T=Spec⁡AT=\Spec A, we may write AA instead of Spec⁡A\Spec A. If s∈Ss\in S, let XsX_{s} be the fiber of X→SX\to S above ss. If moreover CC is a constructible subset of XX, then CTC_{T} denotes the inverse image of CC under XT→XX_{T}\to X, and CsC_{s} is defined similarly.

For a finite-type morphism ϕ:X→Y\phi\colon X\to Y of noetherian schemes with YY irreducible, ϕ\phi is étale over the generic point of YY if and only if ϕ\phi is étale over some dense open V⊂YV\subset Y; in this case, call ϕ\phi generically étale.

3. Reduction to finite fields

We begin the proof of Theorem 1.5 by reducing to the case of a finite field. There exists a finitely generated ℤ\mathbb{Z}-algebra R⊂kR\subset k such that ϕ:X→ℙkn\phi\colon X\to\mathbb{P}^{n}_{k} is the base change of a separated finite-type morphism (denoted using the same letters) ϕ:X→ℙRn\phi\colon X\to\mathbb{P}^{n}_{R}. In the new notation, the original morphism is ϕk:Xk→ℙkn\phi_{k}\colon X_{k}\to\mathbb{P}^{n}_{k}. By shrinking Spec⁡R\Spec R if necessary, we may assume that for each 𝔭∈Spec⁡R\mathfrak{p}\in\Spec R, the fiber X𝔭X_{\mathfrak{p}} is geometrically irreducible [4]*9.7.7(i), the nonempty fibers of ϕ𝔭\phi_{\mathfrak{p}} all have the same dimension [4]*9.2.6(iv), and dimϕ𝔭​(X𝔭)=dimϕk​(Xk)\dim\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}(X_{\mathfrak{p}})=\dim\phi_{k}(X_{k}).

Let ℳbad⊂ℙˇRn\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}}\subset\check{\mathbb{P}}^{n}_{R} be the subset parametrizing hyperplanes HH such that ϕ−1​H\phi^{-1}H is not geometrically irreducible; since the ϕ−1​H\phi^{-1}H are the fibers of a family, ℳbad\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}} is constructible [4]*9.7.7(i). If we prove Theorem 1.5 for a finite ground field, so that dim(ℳbad)𝔭≤codim⁡ϕ𝔭​(X𝔭)+1\dim\,(\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{bad}})_{\mathfrak{p}}\leq\codim\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}(X_{\mathfrak{p}})+1 for every closed point 𝔭\mathfrak{p}, then dim(ℳbad)k≤codim⁡ϕk​(Xk)+1\dim\,(\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}})_{k}\leq\codim\phi_{k}(X_{k})+1 too. Therefore from now on we assume that kk is finite.

4. Random hyperplane slicing

The following lemma is purely set-theoretic; for the time being, XX is just a set.

Lemma 4.1.

Let ϕ:X→ℙn​(𝔽q)\phi\colon X\to\mathbb{P}^{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}) be a map of sets for some n≥1n\geq 1. Let ss be an upper bound on the size of its fibers. For a ((set-theoretic)) hyperplane H⊂ℙn​(𝔽q)H\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}) chosen uniformly at random, define the random variable Z:⁣=#(ϕ−1H)Z\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\#(\phi^{-1}H). Then its mean μ\mu and variance σ2\sigma^{2} satisfy

μ\displaystyle\mu =#​X​(q−1+O⁡(q−2))\displaystyle=\#X\,(q^{-1}+O(q^{-2}))
σ2\displaystyle\sigma^{2} =O⁡(#⁡(ϕ⁡(X))​s2​q−1).\displaystyle=O(\#(\phi(X))\,s^{2}q^{-1}).
Proof.

For any y∈ℙn​(𝔽q)y\in\mathbb{P}^{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}), define

p1:⁣=Prob(y∈H)=qn−1qn+1−1=q−1+O(q−2).p_{1}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\Prob(y\in H)=\frac{q^{n}-1}{q^{n+1}-1}=q^{-1}+O(q^{-2}).

Similarly, for any distinct y,z∈ℙn​(𝔽q)y,z\in\mathbb{P}^{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}), define

p2:⁣=Prob(y,z∈H)=qn−1−1qn+1−1=q−2+O(q−3).p_{2}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\Prob(y,z\in H)=\frac{q^{n-1}-1}{q^{n+1}-1}=q^{-2}+O(q^{-3}).

The mean of ZZ is

μ\displaystyle\mu =𝔼​Z=∑x∈XProb⁡(ϕ⁡(x)∈H)=(#​X)​p1=#​X​(q−1+O⁡(q−2)),\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}Z=\sum_{x\in X}\Prob(\phi(x)\in H)=(\#X)\,p_{1}=\#X\,(q^{-1}+O(q^{-2})),
and the variance is
σ2\displaystyle\sigma^{2} =𝔼⁡(Z2)−(𝔼​Z)2\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}(Z^{2})-(\mathbb{E}Z)^{2}
=∑u,v∈X(Prob⁡(ϕ⁡(u),ϕ⁡(v)∈H)−Prob⁡(ϕ⁡(u)∈H)​Prob⁡(ϕ⁡(v)∈H))\displaystyle=\sum_{u,v\in X}\biggl(\Prob(\phi(u),\phi(v)\in H)-\Prob(\phi(u)\in H)\;\Prob(\phi(v)\in H)\biggr)
=∑ϕ⁡(u)=ϕ⁡(v)(p1−p12)+∑ϕ⁡(u)≠ϕ⁡(v)(p2−p12)\displaystyle=\sum_{\phi(u)=\phi(v)}\left(p_{1}-p_{1}^{2}\right)+\sum_{\phi(u)\neq\phi(v)}\left(p_{2}-p_{1}^{2}\right)
≤∑ϕ⁡(u)=ϕ⁡(v)p1+∑ϕ⁡(u)≠ϕ⁡(v)0(we have p2<p12 since (qn+1−1)2​(p12−p2)=qn−1​(q−1)2)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\phi(u)=\phi(v)}p_{1}+\sum_{\phi(u)\neq\phi(v)}0\quad\textup{(we have $p_{2}<p_{1}^{2}$ since $(q^{n+1}-1)^{2}(p_{1}^{2}-p_{2})=q^{n-1}(q-1)^{2}$)}
≤∑y∈ϕ⁡(X)#​(ϕ−1​y)2​p1\displaystyle\leq\sum_{y\in\phi(X)}\#(\phi^{-1}y)^{2}\,p_{1}
=O⁡(#⁡(ϕ⁡(X))​s2​q−1).∎\displaystyle=O(\#(\phi(X))\,s^{2}q^{-1}).\qed

5. The Lang–Weil bound

We will apply Lemma 4.1 when ϕ\phi comes from a morphism of varieties over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, so we need bounds on the number of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-points of a variety. Throughout the rest of this paper, the implied constant in a big-OO depends on the geometric complexity11 1 Say that a variety is of complexity ≤M\leq M if it is a union of ≤M\leq M open subschemes, each cut out by ≤M\leq M polynomials of degree ≤M\leq M in 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} for some n≤Mn\leq M, with each pair of subschemes glued along ≤M\leq M open sets D⁡(f)D(f) with each ff given by a polynomial of degree ≤M\leq M, with each gluing isomorphism defined by polynomials of degree ≤M\leq M. but not on qq.

Theorem 5.1 ([7]).

Let XX be a variety over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. Let r=dimXr=\dim X.

  1. (a)

    We have #​X​(𝔽q)=O⁡(qr)\#X(\mathbb{F}_{q})=O(q^{r}).

  2. (b)

    If XX is geometrically irreducible, then #​X​(𝔽q)=qr+O⁡(qr−1/2)\#X(\mathbb{F}_{q})=q^{r}+O(q^{r-1/2}).

  3. (c)

    More generally, if aa is the number of irreducible components of XX that are geometrically irreducible of dimension rr, then #​X​(𝔽q)=a​qr+O⁡(qr−1/2)\#X(\mathbb{F}_{q})=aq^{r}+O(q^{r-1/2}).

Proof.

Parts (a) and (b) are Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 in [7]. As is well-known, (c) follows from (a) and (b), since if ZZ is an irreducible component that is not geometrically irreducible, then Z⁡(𝔽q)Z(\mathbb{F}_{q}) is contained in the intersection of the geometric components of ZZ, which is of lower dimension. ∎

6. Counting very bad hyperplanes

Consider a finite field 𝔽q⊃k\mathbb{F}_{q}\supset k. Call a hyperplane H∈ℙˇn​(𝔽q)H\in\check{\mathbb{P}}^{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}) very bad if the number of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-irreducible components of ϕ−1​H\phi^{-1}H that are geometrically irreducible is not 11. The bound on the variance in Lemma 4.1 will bound the number of very bad hyperplanes, because each such hyperplane contributes noticeably to the variance.

Lemma 6.1.

Let XX be a geometrically irreducible variety over a finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} with a morphism ϕ:X→ℙn\phi\colon X\to\mathbb{P}^{n} whose nonempty fibers are all of the same dimension. Then the number of very bad hyperplanes in ℙˇn​(𝔽q)\check{\mathbb{P}}^{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}) is O⁡(qcodim⁡ϕ⁡(X)+1)O(q^{\codim\phi(X)+1}).

Proof.

Let Y=ϕ⁡(X)¯Y=\overline{\phi(X)}. Let r=dimXr=\dim X and m=dimYm=\dim Y, so the nonempty fibers of ϕ\phi have dimension r−mr-m. Consider the random variable #⁡(ϕ−1​H)​(𝔽q)\#(\phi^{-1}H)(\mathbb{F}_{q}) for HH chosen uniformly at random in ℙˇn​(𝔽q)\check{\mathbb{P}}^{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}). Let μ\mu and σ2\sigma^{2} denote its mean and variance. By Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 5.1(a,b) applied to XX, YY, and the fibers of ϕ\phi,

(1) μ\displaystyle\mu =(qr+O⁡(qr−1/2))​(q−1+O⁡(q−2))=qr−1+O⁡(qr−3/2)\displaystyle=(q^{r}+O(q^{r-1/2}))(q^{-1}+O(q^{-2}))=q^{r-1}+O(q^{r-3/2})
(2) σ2\displaystyle\sigma^{2} =O⁡(qm​q2​(r−m)​q−1)=O⁡(q2​r−m−1).\displaystyle=O(q^{m}q^{2(r-m)}q^{-1})=O(q^{2r-m-1}).

If HH is very bad, then ϕ−1​H≠X\phi^{-1}H\neq X, so each irreducible component of ϕ−1​H\phi^{-1}H has dimension r−1r-1, and Theorem 5.1(c) implies that #⁡(ϕ−1​H)​(𝔽q)\#(\phi^{-1}H)(\mathbb{F}_{q}) is either O⁡(qr−3/2)O(q^{r-3/2}) or at least 2​qr−1−O⁡(qr−3/2)2q^{r-1}-O(q^{r-3/2}), so by (1),

|#⁡(ϕ−1​H)​(𝔽q)−μ|≥qr−1−O⁡(qr−3/2)≥12​qr−1for large q.|\#(\phi^{-1}H)(\mathbb{F}_{q})-\mu|\geq q^{r-1}-O(q^{r-3/2})\geq\frac{1}{2}q^{r-1}\quad\textup{for large $q$}.

Define tt so that 12​qr−1=t​σ\dfrac{1}{2}q^{r-1}=t\sigma. Then

Prob​(H​is very bad)\displaystyle\text{Prob}\left(H\ \text{is very bad}\right) ≤Prob​(|#⁡(ϕ−1​H)​(𝔽q)−μ|≥t​σ)\displaystyle\leq\text{Prob}\left(|\#(\phi^{-1}H)(\mathbb{F}_{q})-\mu|\geq t\sigma\right)
≤1t2(by Chebyshev’s inequality)\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{t^{2}}\quad\text{(by Chebyshev's inequality)}
=4​σ2q2​r−2\displaystyle=\frac{4\sigma^{2}}{q^{2r-2}}
=O(q1−m)(by (2)).\displaystyle=O(q^{1-m})\quad\textup{(by \eqref{E:variance using Lang-Weil})}.

Multiplying by the total number of hyperplanes over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, which is O⁡(qn)O(q^{n}), gives O⁡(qn−m+1)O(q^{n-m+1}). ∎

Lemma 6.2.

Let ψ:V→B\psi\colon V\to B be a morphism of varieties over a finite field kk. Suppose that BB is irreducible, and the generic fiber of ψ\psi is not geometrically irreducible. Call a point b∈B⁡(𝔽q)b\in B(\mathbb{F}_{q}) very bad if the number of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-irreducible components of ψ−1​b\psi^{-1}b that are geometrically irreducible is not 11. Then there exists c>0c>0 such that there exist arbitrarily large finite fields 𝔽q⊃k\mathbb{F}_{q}\supset k such that B⁡(𝔽q)B(\mathbb{F}_{q}) contains at least c​qdimBcq^{\dim B} very bad points.

Proof.

If B′→BB^{\prime}\to B is a quasi-finite dominant morphism of irreducible varieties, and the result holds for the base change V′→B′V^{\prime}\to B^{\prime} of V→BV\to B, then the result holds for V→BV\to B, because the image under B′→BB^{\prime}\to B of a set of c′​qdimBc^{\prime}q^{\dim B} points of B′​(𝔽q)B^{\prime}(\mathbb{F}_{q}) has size at least c​qdimBcq^{\dim B} for a possibly smaller cc.

Let η\eta be the generic point of BB. All geometric components of ψ−1​η\psi^{-1}\eta are defined over a finite extension K′K^{\prime} of k⁡(B)k(B). By choosing B′→BB^{\prime}\to B as above with k⁡(B′)=K′k(B^{\prime})=K^{\prime}, we may reduce to the case that all irreducible components of ψ−1​η\psi^{-1}\eta are geometrically irreducible. By passing to a finite extension of kk and replacing BB by an irreducible component of the base extension, we may assume also that BB is geometrically irreducible.

If ψ−1​η\psi^{-1}\eta is empty, then there is a dense open subset UU of BB above which the fibers are empty, and #​U​(𝔽q)=qdimB+O⁡(qdimB−1/2)\#U(\mathbb{F}_{q})=q^{\dim B}+O(q^{\dim B-1/2}) by Theorem 5.1(b), so the conclusion holds with c=1/2c=1/2.

Otherwise ψ−1​η\psi^{-1}\eta has ≥2\geq 2 irreducible components. Let W1W_{1} and W2W_{2} be their closures in VV. The locus of b∈Bb\in B such that the fibers of W1→BW_{1}\to B and W2→BW_{2}\to B above bb are distinct geometrically irreducible components of ψ−1​b\psi^{-1}b is constructible, so by replacing BB by a dense open subvariety we may assume that the locus is all of BB. Now for any 𝔽q⊃k\mathbb{F}_{q}\supset k, all b∈B⁡(𝔽q)b\in B(\mathbb{F}_{q}) are very bad, and their number is qdimB+O⁡(qdimB−1/2)q^{\dim B}+O(q^{\dim B-1/2}) by Theorem 5.1(b). ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.5.

By Section 3, we may assume that the ground field is finite. Let BB be an irreducible variety contained in ℳbad\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}}. Let V→BV\to B be the morphism whose fiber over a point corresponding to a hyperplane HH is ϕ−1​H\phi^{-1}H. By Lemma 6.2, for arbitrarily large qq there are at least c​qdimBcq^{\dim B} very bad hyperplanes H∈B⁡(𝔽q)H\in B(\mathbb{F}_{q}). On the other hand, by Lemma 6.1 there are at most O⁡(qcodim⁡Y+1)O(q^{\codim Y+1}) very bad hyperplanes. Thus dimB≤codim⁡Y+1\dim B\leq\codim Y+1. Since this holds for all irreducible B⊂ℳbadB\subset\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}}, we obtain dimℳbad≤codim⁡Y+1\dim\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}}\leq\codim Y+1. ∎

7. Proof of the most general version

Lemma 7.1.

For a constructible set Y⊂ℙnY\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}, the locus of hyperplanes containing YY is a variety of dimension at most codim⁡Y−1\codim Y-1.

Proof.

Let LL be the linear span of YY in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}. The hyperplanes containing YY are those containing LL, which form a projective space of dimension codim⁡L−1≤codim⁡Y−1\codim L-1\leq\codim Y-1. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.8.

We may assume that kk is algebraically closed. By Lemma 7.1, we may ignore hyperplanes HH containing ϕ⁡(X)\phi(X). Now every irreducible component of ϕ−1​H\phi^{-1}H is of dimension dimX−1\dim X-1. Let X′=X−WX^{\prime}=X-W. By Theorem 1.5 applied to X′→ℙnX^{\prime}\to\mathbb{P}^{n}, it suffices to consider HH such that ϕ−1​H∩X′\phi^{-1}H\cap X^{\prime} is geometrically irreducible. For such HH, the following are equivalent:

  • •

    H∈ℳbadH\in\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{bad}}};

  • •

    ϕ−1​H\phi^{-1}H is not irreducible;

  • •

    ϕ−1​H\phi^{-1}H contains a closed subset of WW of dimension dimX−1\dim X-1;

  • •

    ϕ−1​H\phi^{-1}H contains WiW_{i} for some ii;

  • •

    HH contains ϕ⁡(Wi)\phi(W_{i}) for some ii.∎

8. Application to monodromy

Let KK be a field. Fix a separable closure KsK_{s} of KK, and let GK=Gal⁡(Ks/K)G_{K}=\Gal(K_{s}/K). If f:X→Spec⁡Kf\colon X\to\Spec K is finite étale, let Mon⁡(f)\Mon(f) be the image of GK→Aut⁡(X⁡(Ks))G_{K}\to\Aut(X(K_{s})). More generally, if f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y is generically étale with YY irreducible, let fK:XK→Spec⁡Kf_{K}\colon X_{K}\to\Spec K be the generic fiber, and define the monodromy group Mon(X/Y)=Mon(f):⁣=Mon(fK)\Mon(X/Y)=\Mon(f)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\Mon(f_{K}).

Let f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y be a degree dd finite étale morphism of schemes. As in [10]*Section 3.5, define the Galois scheme of ff as the following open and closed YY-subscheme of the ddth fibered power X×Y⋯×YXX\times_{Y}\dots\times_{Y}X:

GS(f):={(x1,…,xd)∈X×Y⋯×YX∣xi≠xjfori≠j}.\GS(f):=\{(x_{1},...,x_{d})\in X\times_{Y}\dots\times_{Y}X\mid x_{i}\neq x_{j}\ \textup{for}\ i\neq j\}.

If L/KL/K is a finite separable extension, with Galois closure L~\widetilde{L}, and ff is Spec⁡L→Spec⁡K\Spec L\to\Spec K, then Mon⁡(f)≃Gal⁡(L~/K)\Mon(f)\simeq\Gal(\widetilde{L}/K) and any connected component ZZ of GS⁡(f)\GS(f) is isomorphic to Spec⁡L~\Spec\widetilde{L}.

Lemma 8.1.

Let f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y be a finite étale morphism with YY irreducible. Let ZZ be a nonempty open and closed subscheme of GS⁡(f)\GS(f). Then Mon⁡(X/Y)≃Mon⁡(Z/Y)\Mon(X/Y)\simeq\Mon(Z/Y).

Proof.

Let K=k⁡(Y)K=k(Y). Then Z⁡(Ks)Z(K_{s}) is a union of one or more GKG_{K}-orbits in the set of bijections {1,…,d}→X⁡(Ks)\{1,\ldots,d\}\to X(K_{s}). Thus GK→Aut⁡(X⁡(Ks))G_{K}\to\Aut(X(K_{s})) and GK→Aut⁡(Z⁡(Ks))G_{K}\to\Aut(Z(K_{s})) have the same kernel, and hence canonically isomorphic images. ∎

Lemma 8.2.

Let f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y be an open morphism of noetherian schemes. Suppose that YY is irreducible, with generic point η\eta. Then there is a bijection Irr⁡X→Irr⁡Xη\Irr X\to\Irr X_{\eta} sending ZZ to ZηZ_{\eta}.

Proof.

If Z∈Irr⁡XZ\in\Irr X, then the set Z′:⁣=X−⋃W∈Irr⁡X,W≠ZW⊂ZZ^{\prime}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}X-\bigcup_{W\in\Irr X,\;W\neq Z}W\subset Z is nonempty and open in XX, so f⁡(Z′)f(Z^{\prime}) is nonempty and open in YY, so η∈f⁡(Z′)⊂f⁡(Z)\eta\in f(Z^{\prime})\subset f(Z), so ZZ meets XηX_{\eta}. By [3]*0, 2.1.13, {Z∈Irr⁡X:Z meets Xη}\{Z\in\Irr X:\textup{$Z$ meets $X_{\eta}$}\} is in bijection with Irr⁡Xη\Irr X_{\eta}. ∎

Lemma 8.3.

Let Z→YZ\to Y be a right GG-torsor for a finite group GG, with YY irreducible and ZZ connected.

  1. (a)

    Let y∈Yy\in Y. Let TT be a connected component of ZyZ_{y}. Let GT⊂GG_{T}\subset G be the decomposition group of TT. Then Mon⁡(T/y)≃GT⊂G\Mon(T/y)\simeq G_{T}\subset G.

  2. (b)

    The injection Mon⁡(T/y)↪G\Mon(T/y)\hookrightarrow G in (a) is an isomorphism if and only if ZyZ_{y} is connected.

  3. (c)

    If ZZ is irreducible, then Mon⁡(Z/Y)​→∼​G\Mon(Z/Y)\overset{\sim}{\rightarrow}G.

Proof.

Part (a) is just the usual theory of the decomposition and inertia groups specialized to the Galois étale case: use [5]*V.1.3 and V.2.4; the residue field extension is Galois. Part (b) follows since GG acts transitively on ZyZ_{y}. Part (c) follows by applying (b) to the generic point η\eta of YY and noting that ZηZ_{\eta} is irreducible by Lemma 8.2. ∎

Corollary 8.4.

Let f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y be a finite étale morphism, where YY is irreducible and normal. Let ZZ be a connected component of GS⁡(f)\GS(f). Let y∈Yy\in Y. Then there is an injection Mon⁡(Xy/y)↪Mon⁡(X/Y)\Mon(X_{y}/y)\hookrightarrow\Mon(X/Y), well-defined up to an inner automorphism of Mon⁡(X/Y)\Mon(X/Y), and it is an isomorphism if and only if ZyZ_{y} is connected.

Proof.

Since YY is normal, ZZ is irreducible. The proof of [2]*Proposition 3.2.10 implies that Z→YZ\to Y is a GG-torsor. Choose a connected component TT of ZyZ_{y}. By Lemma 8.3, we have an injection Mon⁡(T/y)↪G≃Mon⁡(Z/Y)\Mon(T/y)\hookrightarrow G\simeq\Mon(Z/Y) which is an isomorphism if and only if ZyZ_{y} is connected. By Lemma 8.1 applied to Xy→{y}X_{y}\to\{y\} and X→YX\to Y, this injection identifies with Mon⁡(Xy/y)↪Mon⁡(X/Y)\Mon(X_{y}/y)\hookrightarrow\Mon(X/Y). ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.9.

Let V⊂YV\subset Y be the largest normal open subscheme above which ϕ\phi is finite étale. If HH satisfies (i), then (ii) holds if and only if H∩VH\cap V is irreducible. By Theorem 1.1 applied to Y⊂ℙnY\subset\mathbb{P}^{n} and to V⊂ℙnV\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}, we may discard all HH that fail (i) or (ii). Replace X→YX\to Y by ϕ−1​V→V\phi^{-1}V\to V.

Let ZZ be a connected component of GS⁡(ϕ)\GS(\phi), and let ff be the morphism Z→YZ\to Y. For HH such that H∩YH\cap Y is irreducible, let hh denote the generic point of H∩YH\cap Y; then the following are equivalent:

  • •

    H∈ℳgoodH\in\mathcal{M}_{{\operatorname{good}}};

  • •

    Mon⁡(ϕH)​→∼​Mon⁡(ϕ)\Mon(\phi_{H})\overset{\sim}{\rightarrow}\Mon(\phi);

  • •

    Mon⁡(ϕh)​→∼​Mon⁡(ϕ)\Mon(\phi_{h})\overset{\sim}{\rightarrow}\Mon(\phi);

  • •

    ZhZ_{h} is irreducible (by Corollary 8.4);

  • •

    f−1​Hf^{-1}H is irreducible (by Lemma 8.2).

Since YY is normal, ZZ is irreducible, so by Theorem 1.5 applied to ff, the last condition above fails on a constructible locus of dimension at most codim⁡Y+1\codim Y+1. ∎
